HEADLINE:
Aerobic efficiency is solidly in place three weeks out. But the crossing demands loaded, hilly time-on-feet, and the training has none of that. Terrain specificity, not fitness, is the open question.

OVERVIEW:
The running picture is coherent and strong: the recent four-week block nearly doubled the prior stretch, and the easy-run efficiency signal has held clean across the longer efforts, with comparable-effort HR sitting in the lower band. Strength has been steady rather than heavy — the functional sessions are short and low-HR, more circuit-durability than max-load work, which fits a period where running volume is the priority. Step counts remain high enough that background movement is meaningfully padding the daily load beyond what the logged sessions show, and even rest days aren't truly sedentary. What's missing is not effort or consistency but modality: with a self-supported crossing carrying a pack over a mountain border under three weeks away, the training remains almost entirely flat, unloaded road running. The flat cardio-load status is a byproduct of that data stream not capturing this week's work rather than a real absence of training.

TRENDS:
The year-to-date jump over last year is dramatic, and the 16-week shape reads as a genuine build layered on top of a much larger base than this point last season. That build makes sense for a hybrid athlete maintaining year-round readiness — this isn't a taper and doesn't need to be one yet. The shape is a rising, slightly cyclical progression with recovery weeks folded in, which is exactly what sustainable long-term development should look like. The one caveat is that "more running volume" and "more crossing-specific preparation" are not the same trend, and the former has been climbing while the latter hasn't appeared.

THRESHOLD:
The single threshold marker from early July is fast and sits well within this athlete's demonstrated speed range, but with no 30-day baseline yet it's a point, not a trajectory. For the crossing, threshold pace is largely academic — the event is a multi-day sub-threshold grind, and current aerobic efficiency at easy paces is the far more relevant readout. That efficiency is holding, which is the reassuring part. Speed capacity is clearly intact; it just isn't the quality this next block hinges on.

ZONES:
The recent sessions distribute sensibly — the longer runs are sitting predominantly in Z1–Z2 with only token Z3, which is the correct signature for durability work and matches the block's intent. The one genuinely mixed session earlier in the month had real Z3 time and a higher average, a deliberate faster effort rather than grey-zone drift. There's no meaningful accumulation of unproductive middle-intensity work across the recent runs; easy is staying easy and the harder day was clearly harder. For what this phase is trying to build, the polarisation is appropriate.

HR_COMPARISON:
The strength sessions read as low-intensity throughout, avg HR sitting comfortably in the lower zones with brief excursions — consistent with circuit-style functional work rather than heavy loading, which is worth naming only because it means strength isn't currently contributing much systemic stress on top of the running. The one long-run HR estimate earlier in the month ran higher than the surrounding chest-strap runs, but the more recent efforts agree well with the established easy-run band, so there's no source-disagreement worth worrying about.

CALENDAR:
The running and strength cadence has been reliably interleaved — runs and functional sessions alternating without long gaps — which is the real story behind the consistency, more than the streak length itself. What the calendar doesn't show is variety of stimulus: every logged run is a Copenhagen or Furesø road/path outing. For an athlete about to spend nine days on hilly self-supported trail, the uniformity of the training environment is the pattern to notice.

PERSONAL_BESTS:
Nothing on the road-PB front is the priority right now, and none of the existing bests are in play during a block oriented toward a long slow crossing. The 50K/ultra best is the relevant reference, and the current base clearly exceeds where it was set — but that best came with far more time-on-feet specificity than the current road-heavy weeks provide.

WATCH:
- Watch whether any loaded-pack or sustained-climb sessions enter the training before the crossing — the specificity gap is the one genuinely open variable.
- Watch how the body responds to back-to-back days as the event nears, since multi-day durability, not single-run pace, is what the crossing tests.
- Watch whether easy-run HR stays in its current lower band as volume tapers toward the start.
- Note sleep has been erratic across recent weeks; worth keeping an eye on as pre-event load settles, without reading too much into it yet.

HEADLINE:
Efficiency continues to hold across varied terrain and distances. Recovery signals (Polar strain/tolerance, sleep) look rough, but volume and pace tell a steadier story. Real gap remains: nothing yet resembles loaded, sustained climbing.

OVERVIEW:
The week closes with a short, easy 11 km sitting comfortably in the low HR band, consistent with the pattern across the 20 km and 12 km efforts either side of it — genuine aerobic efficiency, not just a quiet taper day. Strength frequency remains solid within the 4-week window, with sessions trending toward shorter durations and consistently low HR, suggesting these are settling into maintenance-mode rather than progressive overload right now. Steps remain high on both training and rest days, which continues to support the case that background activity (commute, daily movement) is doing real aerobic work the run log alone doesn't capture. The Polar-reported detraining status is worth noting but shouldn't be taken at face value — it reflects a zeroed short-term strain reading against a real 28-day tolerance base, and doesn't square with the volume, pace or strength consistency actually on display this week.

TRENDS:
The 16-week shape shows a clear step up in volume over the last month relative to the prior four weeks, and the year-to-date comparison against last year is stark — this is a training year built on a fundamentally different base than 2025. That's consistent with someone deliberately building durable aerobic capacity rather than chasing a single peak, which fits the standing philosophy. The current picture reads as consolidation after a genuine volume jump, not plateau or irregularity — the kind of pattern you'd want to see heading into a long, unsupported effort.

THRESHOLD:
The one threshold data point this cycle sits at a strong pace-to-HR ratio, and the surrounding easy-run HR trend — consistently lower than prior blocks at comparable paces — supports the idea that aerobic economy has genuinely shifted, not just that the threshold test happened to land well. Without a fresh 30-day baseline it's hard to quantify the magnitude of the shift, but directionally everything agrees.

ZONES:
Recent runs sit overwhelmingly in Z1–Z2, with only brief, incidental excursions into Z3 — exactly the distribution you'd want from a block built around efficiency and durability rather than sharpening. The 07-12 session stands out with more sustained Z2/Z3 time at a higher average HR, a legitimate harder effort among otherwise conservative sessions. Strength sessions are living almost entirely in Z1, which is expected and appropriate given their role here isn't cardiovascular.

HR_COMPARISON:
Strength-session HR continues to sit low and stable across the block, with no session pushing meaningfully into Z2 for long — consistent with functional/maintenance-style work rather than metabolically demanding circuits. Nothing in the run-versus-strength HR comparison this week stands out as inconsistent or worth flagging beyond what's already been said about easy-run efficiency.

CALENDAR:
Running frequency has held at a genuinely elevated cadence through the past month compared to the prior four weeks, and the streak context (23 weeks running, 6 weeks strength) shows this isn't a short-lived spike — it's a sustained shift in habitual load. That consistency, more than any single session, is probably the strongest evidence for the efficiency gains being real rather than noise.

PERSONAL_BESTS:
Nothing in the current training — dominated by easy-to-moderate aerobic volume — is pointed at a short-distance PB attempt right now, and that's appropriate given the near-term focus is elsewhere. The existing 50K and marathon bests remain the more relevant reference points given the terrain and duration of what's coming.

WATCH:
- Whether any pack-loaded or sustained-climb sessions get introduced before the crossing, given the terrain mismatch already identified.
- Whether the Polar strain reading recovers with continued activity or continues to read oddly against actual training consistency.
- Sleep duration and score variability night-to-night — worth monitoring simply as background context heading into a long, physically demanding stretch.
- Whether strength sessions stay in maintenance mode or pick back up in duration/intensity once the crossing is behind you.

HEADLINE:
Aerobic efficiency is locked in and back-to-back durability is proven. With St. Olavsleden two weeks out, the taper window has arrived — and loaded, sustained-climb specificity never entered the picture.

OVERVIEW:
The recent four-week block landed a substantial volume jump while holding easy-run HR in its lower band, which is exactly what you want going into a multi-day self-supported effort — the durability base is real, not borrowed. Strength has stayed frequent through the same window, sitting almost entirely in low zones, so it's supporting the running rather than competing with it. Steps remain very high even on rest days, meaning your true daily load is higher than the run log alone suggests, and that background time-on-feet matters more than usual for what's coming. The one genuine gap remains terrain: none of this volume carried a loaded pack or sustained climbing, so the crossing's specific demand is still untested. Recovery signals are mixed and the cardio-load status reads as detraining, which almost certainly reflects a real recent drop in logged running — appropriate this close to the start, not a concern.

TRENDS:
The 16-week shape is clearly a build-then-consolidate rhythm rather than a flat plateau, and the year-to-date jump against the same point last year is enormous — you're operating in a completely different volume tier than a year ago. That trajectory makes sense for someone building durable year-round hybrid capacity, and the recent block's expansion followed by an easing edge fits a deliberate approach to the event window rather than any loss of momentum.

THRESHOLD:
Threshold pace remains sharp from the early-July measurement, and there's no signal it's eroded — the easy work has been protecting aerobic fitness, not blunting it. But with insufficient rolling baseline history, treat the single figure as a reference point rather than a trend. For the crossing, threshold speed isn't the limiter anyway; sustained low-intensity economy over days is, and that's the quality your recent runs actually demonstrate.

ZONES:
The distribution is strongly aerobic, which is right for this phase — the long runs and easy sessions sit predominantly in Z1–Z2 with only brief excursions higher. The per-session shapes confirm it: your recent long and mid-distance runs are genuinely steady, not disguised interval sessions, with only the earlier faster session carrying meaningful Z3 time. That's the appropriate texture heading into a self-supported multi-day effort where control, not intensity, is the skill being rehearsed.

HR_COMPARISON:
Strength sessions continue to sit low and steady, confirming these are functional/conditioning-flavoured rather than maximal-load days — sensible alongside the running volume. The two most recent strength sessions carry no HR at all, so there's less to read there, but nothing in the pattern suggests strength work is adding hidden cardiovascular strain. Sensor sources agree well enough across runs that effort judgements hold regardless of origin.

CALENDAR:
The mix of running and strength across the block shows a well-distributed week rather than clustering, and the back-to-back-capable spacing has quietly built the multi-day tolerance the crossing needs. The strength cadence has held its own rhythm alongside running without either crowding the other — a sign the schedule is genuinely sustainable rather than propped up by good weeks.

PERSONAL_BESTS:
Your standing 5K through Half bests were all set in a faster-focused window last year, and current training is deliberately pointed elsewhere — endurance economy, not top-end speed — so none are realistic targets in this window, nor should they be. The relevant "best" right now is durability over consecutive days, which won't show on the PB board but is exactly what you're sharpening.

WATCH:
- Watch whether any loaded-pack or elevation-heavy session appears before the start — still the single open variable, and the last realistic window to touch it is closing.
- Watch how easy-run HR behaves as logged volume drops into the taper; a continued low band confirms freshness rather than lost stimulus.
- Watch that the taper doesn't over-shed — the goal is arriving fresh, not detrained, so some quality time-on-feet should remain.
- Keep a loose eye on recovery consistency as pre-event logistics build; erratic patterns are worth noting but not overreacting to this close in.
